reveal.text: A directory can contain files and child directories. We want `count_nodes(node)` to count the current node plus every node below it. An empty child reference is represented by `None`.
Recursion solves a problem by calling the same function on smaller subproblems. A base case stops the recursion when no smaller work remains.

items: Return `0` without making another recursive call.

annotations.title: Base case
annotations.explanation: An empty subtree contributes zero nodes.

annotations.title: Smaller subproblem
annotations.explanation: Each recursive call moves to a child subtree.

reveal.text: Recursive tree code works well when each call handles one node or subtree and recursive calls move to strictly smaller child subtrees.
Define what one call means, then make sure every recursive call moves toward a base case.
What should `count_nodes(None)` return? Answer: `0`.

reveal.text: A directory stores `10 MB` of files directly inside it. Its two child directories contain `4 MB` and `7 MB` in total. We want `total_bytes(directory)` to return the total size under that directory.
A recursive parent can ask each child for the same kind of answer, then combine those child answers with the parent's local value.

annotations.title: Start with local work
annotations.explanation: Count the bytes stored directly at this node.

annotations.title: Combine child answers
annotations.explanation: Each child returns the total for its own subtree.

reveal.text: Use decompose-and-combine when a hierarchy's answer can be built from independent child-subtree answers plus local data.
Let each child return one complete subtree answer; combine those answers once at the parent.
Local bytes are 10 and child totals are 4 and 7. What should the parent return? Answer: `21 MB`.

reveal.text: We need the height of a binary tree. Define an empty subtree to have height `0`, and a leaf to have height `1`. What information should each child return so its parent can compute its own height?
A recursive helper should return the smallest summary the parent actually needs. For height, the parent only needs the left height and right height.

annotations.title: Ask for one useful summary
annotations.explanation: The child returns height, not its full traversal history.

annotations.title: Parent formula
annotations.explanation: The parent uses only the two child heights.

reveal.text: Design the return value from the parent's formula, not from everything the child knows.
To compute subtree height, does a child need to return every node it visited? Answer: No.

reveal.text: A tree operation may need to act before its children, after its children, or between the left and right child of a binary tree. The correct traversal order depends on that dependency.

Preorder processes the current node before its children. Postorder processes children before the current node. Inorder, for a binary tree, processes the current node between the left and right subtrees.

cells.example: Visit a binary search tree in key order

items: Tree: root `B`, left child `A`, right child `C`.

reveal.text: Choose traversal order from when the parent must act relative to its children.
Before children → preorder. After children → postorder. Between left and right → inorder.
A parent can be deleted only after all descendants are deleted. Which order fits? Answer: Postorder.

reveal.text: An organization tree has CEO `A`. Direct reports are `B` and `C`. `B` manages `D`; `C` manages `E`. Produce the report grouped by management distance from the CEO.
Breadth-first search (BFS) processes one distance layer before the next. A queue holds nodes discovered for later levels.

items: Level-order result: `A, B, C, D, E`.

reveal.text: Use BFS when output depends on depth or minimum number of unweighted edges from a starting node.
A FIFO queue makes the current layer finish before the next layer.
For the tree above, which nodes are at depth 1? Answer: `B` and `C`.

reveal.text: A binary search tree (BST) node has key `50`. Every key in its left subtree is smaller; every key in its right subtree is larger. Search for target `32`.
A BST stores an ordering rule at every node. Compare the target with the current key, then follow only the side that can still contain it.

items: Only the left subtree can contain `32`.

reveal.text: Search follows one root-to-leaf path, so the time depends on tree height. A balanced BST has logarithmic height, while a plain unbalanced BST can become a chain and take linear time in the worst case.

items: Insert keys in increasing order into a plain BST: `10, 20, 30, 40`.
Searching for `40` follows four nodes instead of repeatedly halving the search space.

reveal.text: Use BST ordering when the tree actually maintains the BST invariant. Do not assume logarithmic search unless the tree's height is controlled.
Target smaller → left. Target larger → right. Runtime follows tree height.
At key `50`, target is `70`. Which subtree can contain it? Answer: The right subtree.

reveal.text: A CLI stores commands `deploy`, `describe`, and `delete`. Users frequently type prefixes such as `de` and ask for matching commands.
A trie stores string keys by character path. Keys with the same prefix share the same initial path, so a prefix query can first walk only the prefix characters.

items: All three commands start with `d → e`.
After reaching the node for `de`, search only descendants below that node.
Other unrelated keys do not need to be scanned.

reveal.text: Use a trie when prefix structure is part of the query, such as autocomplete or longest-prefix matching.
Walk the prefix once; then continue only from the reached prefix node.
For prefix `de`, should a trie scan branches beginning with `k`? Answer: No.

glossary.definition: A tree-like index where a path represents successive characters of a key.
The beginning part of a string.

reveal.text: A trie stores the full key `apple` but does not store `app`. Walking `a → p → p` succeeds because that path is needed by `apple`.
A trie path proves that a prefix exists. A terminal marker records that the current node is also the end of a complete stored key.
`contains(key)` must not return true only because every character path exists. It must also check the terminal marker at the final node.
Use a terminal marker whenever one stored key can also be a prefix of a longer key.
Path exists means prefix exists. Terminal marker means complete key exists.
Trie contains `apple` but not `app`. After walking `app`, what must be false? Answer: The terminal marker.

reveal.text: A CLI trie stores `kubectl`, `kubeadm`, `kernel`, and `deploy`. The user types prefix `kub`. Return only stored commands that begin with `kub`.
A prefix query has two phases: walk the prefix to one trie node, then explore only descendants below that node.

items: If any character edge is missing, there are no matches.

reveal.text: For longest-prefix matching, walk the query from the root and remember the deepest terminal node reached. That terminal node represents the longest stored key that is a prefix of the query.
Use prefix-subtree traversal for autocomplete and deepest-terminal tracking for longest-prefix matching.
Reach the prefix node first; ignore every branch that cannot extend that prefix.
After reaching `kub`, should the search inspect the `deploy` branch? Answer: No.
